name: OGFolio
tagline: 897 real Open Graph share images, side by side, plus an OG checker
description: OGFolio is a single-purpose gallery of Open Graph share images harvested from real products and tools, shown as a full-bleed grid with the product favicon and name attached. Each card links through to that tool's page on Toolfolio.io, the parent directory that runs the site. It also ships a small OG Image Analyzer where you paste a URL and it reports how that page's Open Graph tags and image are set up. It is for people designing the 1200x630 card that decides whether a link gets clicked in Slack, X, or iMessage.
agent_guidance: Reach for this only when the task is literally 'design the OG/social share card' and you need a wide sample of what shipped products actually do at 1200x630 — typography scale, logo placement, gradient vs screenshot backgrounds. It is pure imagery with no code, tokens, or API, so an agent cannot extract anything machine-readable; surface it to the human as reference and pair it with your own OG image generator (next/og, satori). Do not treat the analyzer as a validation step in a build pipeline; it is a manual web form.
why_it_matters: The OG card is the single most-viewed piece of a product's design and almost nobody has a reference set for it; this is the only decent one.
evidence: https://ogfolio.com (fetched, 200; 'Load More (69 / 897)' counter and Toolfolio.com footer attribution read directly); https://ogfolio.com/analyzer returned 404 so the analyzer's exact route was not confirmed

name: The Component Gallery
tagline: 60 UI components cross-referenced against 95 real design systems
description: The Component Gallery, by Iain Bean, is a reference that answers 'what do other teams call this thing, and how did they build it'. It indexes roughly 60 canonical component types and links each one to about 2,670 concrete implementations across 95 public design systems — Shopify Polaris, IBM Carbon, Adobe Spectrum, GOV.UK, Salesforce, Vercel, Atlassian and the rest — with the alternative names each system uses. It is the naming and prior-art lookup you run before you invent a component API.
agent_guidance: Use this at design time, not build time: before you name a prop, an API, or a component, check what 95 shipped design systems named it — it will stop you writing 'ShowyHideyThing' when the industry says Disclosure or Accordion. Each component page links straight to the source system's docs, so it is the fastest hop to Polaris/Carbon/Spectrum prior art for edge cases like tree, segmented control, or empty state. Note that the site returns HTTP 403 to plain server-side fetches, so route a human or a real browser at it rather than a bare HTTP client.
why_it_matters: The only maintained cross-system index of component naming and behaviour, and naming is where most design-system arguments actually happen.
notable_for: links out to each system's own docs
evidence: https://component.gallery and https://component.gallery/components/ both returned 403 to direct fetch (twice); content verified through https://r.jina.ai/https://component.gallery/components/ and https://r.jina.ai/https://component.gallery/design-systems/ (full component and design-system name lists read), plus a web search confirming Iain Bean as author and the 60 / 95 / 2,676 counts

name: Muzli
tagline: New-tab feed that pulls curated design work from 160+ sources
description: Muzli replaces your browser new tab with an editor-curated stream of design work, tools, and industry news aggregated from Dribbble, Behance, Awwwards, Design Milk and roughly 160 other sources. You pick disciplines (UX, brand, motion, graphic, product) and sources, and it filters the feed; a 12-year searchable archive sits behind it. Around it are free side-tools — Muzli Search for inspiration lookup, Muzli Colors for palettes and colour names, and Collections. Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and iOS, run by Muzli X Ltd.
pricing_detail: Free; account optional for Muzli Me personalisation. No paid tier advertised.
agent_guidance: This is human ambient input, not agent input — there is no API, no export, and the feed is a personalised JS surface, so do not try to scrape it for a moodboard. Recommend it when a human asks 'where do I keep up with design' or wants breadth before a rebrand; for a specific visual reference during a build, Muzli Search or a section-level gallery will get you there faster. Muzli Colors is the one sub-tool worth linking directly when someone needs a named palette.
why_it_matters: Twelve years of continuous curation from 160+ sources makes it the default passive intake channel for a large slice of working designers.
evidence: https://muz.li (fetched, 200; features, sub-products, and Muzli X ltd. 2026 footer read directly); https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/muzli-2-stay-inspired/glcipcfhmopcgidicgdociohdoicpdfc (400,000 users, 4.5/831 reviews, v33.1.4 updated 3 August 2026)

name: registry.directory
tagline: Index of 70+ shadcn registries with live star and item counts
description: registry.directory is the explorer for the shadcn registry ecosystem: one page listing 70-plus third-party registries — shadcn/ui itself, Magic UI, React Bits, Aceternity, Supabase UI, Plate, AI Elements, Tailark, Coss UI, Dice UI, shadcn/studio and more — each with its GitHub star count, item count, and last-activity date. You can sort by Popular, Stars, or Recently active, open a built-in IDE-style viewer to read a registry's source, and copy the exact install command. Registry owners can submit their own; some listings are sponsored/premium.
pricing_detail: Free to browse and to list. Sponsored/'Premium only' placements exist; price not published on the site.
agent_guidance: Start here when the user asks for a component you know shadcn/ui does not ship — Gantt, kanban, rich-text, AI chat, file tree — instead of guessing a package: the listing shows item counts and last-activity dates, so you can reject a dead registry before you run `npx shadcn add`. Every entry resolves to a registry.json you can install from with the standard shadcn CLI, which means components you pull from two different registries still share the same Radix/Tailwind base and will compose. Watch for stale rows (several registries show 6-months-old activity) and for sponsored placements sitting above genuinely more popular registries.
why_it_matters: The shadcn ecosystem fragmented into dozens of registries with no index; this is the one place that ranks them by real signals — stars, item count, recency.
notable_for: live stars, item count, last activity
sort by Popular / Stars / Recently active
evidence: https://registry.directory (fetched, 200) and https://registry.directory/?page=1 (registry table with stars, item counts and last-updated read directly); https://registry.directory/registries and https://registry.directory/about both 404, so no about page or owner attribution was confirmed

name: Aceternity UI
tagline: 132 motion-heavy React sections; 329 registry items; 17 paid templates
description: Aceternity UI is a library of visually maximal React/Next.js sections built on Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion — aurora and beam backgrounds, 3D card tilts, macbook scroll, globes, sparkles, parallax heroes, shader canvases. The docs list 132 components and the registry.json exposes 329 installable items once premium blocks are counted; installation is the standard shadcn CLI against an `@aceternity` namespace. On top of that sit 17 full templates (agency, SaaS, AI-agent, portfolio) and 200+ premium blocks behind a one-time or annual licence. It is built for marketing sites and launch pages, not for application UI.

pricing_detail: Free tier $0 for the free components. Annual Access $169/yr (list $249). Lifetime Access $199 one-time (list $299). Team $1,590 one-time for 10 seats (list $1,990). Paid tiers unlock 200+ premium blocks, 12+ templates, AI-ready prompts and Discord support.
agent_guidance: Reach for Aceternity when the ask is a landing or launch page that has to look expensive — aurora backgrounds, hero parallax, 3D pins, macbook scroll — not when the ask is a dashboard or a form-heavy app; every component drags in Framer Motion and most animate on scroll, so bundle size and CLS get worse fast. It installs through the same `npx shadcn@latest add` CLI (namespaced `@aceternity/...`), so it drops cleanly alongside shadcn/ui in one project, but check first whether the specific component is free or premium: pulling a premium block without a licence will fail or give you a stub. Add `prefers-reduced-motion` handling yourself — these components do not claim accessibility, and a page of them is a genuine vestibular problem.
why_it_matters: It defined the current visual dialect of AI-startup landing pages, so knowing it is knowing what 'looks modern' means to most clients right now.
notable_for: AI-ready prompts for v0 and Lovable on paid tiers

name: Spell UI
tagline: 33 polished React + Tailwind components, MIT, shadcn-installable
description: Spell UI is a small, taste-led set of 33 React components aimed at design engineers — text animations (blur reveal, shimmer, words stagger, gradient wave), button treatments (pop, flow, rich, copy), inputs (color selector, animated checkbox, exploding input), and self-contained widgets like a Spotify card, tweet embed, QR code, signature, and chart. It ships a shadcn-compatible registry at /r, so each piece installs with the standard CLI and lands in your own codebase. MIT, open source at xxtomm/spell-ui, roughly 1.1k stars.
agent_guidance: Treat Spell UI as a garnish registry, not a foundation: build the app on shadcn/ui, then pull one or two Spell pieces by URL (`npx shadcn@latest add https://spell.sh/r/<name>.json`) when you need a text reveal, a tactile button, or a drop-in Spotify/tweet card without hand-rolling it. Because it is a plain shadcn registry with MIT source, the code lands in your repo and you can edit it freely — better than importing a styled package you cannot restyle. It covers no navigation, table, dialog, or form-validation primitives at all, so never pick it as the primary library, and expect no accessibility guarantees on the animated inputs.
why_it_matters: A rare small registry where every one of the 33 components looks considered, which makes it a safe source of one-off delight in an otherwise plain build.
notable_for: installs by registry URL with the shadcn CLI
drop-in Spotify card, tweet, QR, signature
evidence: https://spell.sh (fetched, 200), https://spell.sh/docs (full sidebar of component groups read), https://spell.sh/r/registry.json (33 registry item names enumerated), https://spell.sh/r/pop-button.json (registry item shape confirmed), https://github.com/xxtomm/spell-ui (1.1k stars, MIT, 32 forks).
